overview: The atlas colors an enormous 200 to 100 BCE region “Tungus,” but the label is retrospective and the shape is not a civilization. Its 17-part multipolygon covers the Korean peninsula and islands, southern Primorye, and the Amur corridor. Seoul, Pyongyang, Gyeongju, Jeju, Vladivostok, Khabarovsk, and Komsomolsk all test inside, while Shenyang, Changchun, Harbin, and the upper Amur test outside. No source makes that peculiar border a single state, people, language, or homeland. Modern Tungusic describes related languages; proposed Proto-Tungusic dates and homelands remain debated, and “Tungus” spread through Russian writing many centuries later. Local evidence instead reveals Wiman Joseon and other Korean communities, Krounovka farming settlements in Primorye, and Poltse traditions along the Amur. Houses, heated floors, millet, pigs, fish, pottery, iron, maritime exchange, graves, children, healing, water, and toilets survive unevenly, so this card separates discoveries from careful inference. No securely localized Tungusic writing sample survives from the exact interval. At 100 BCE the atlas deletes the umbrella and leaves former target probes blank; later snapshots add other labels, while families and regional histories continue.

periods.title: 200 to 190 BCE: one imported color, many regional histories
periods.summary: The atlas introduces its vast Tungus multipolygon at 200 BCE. Archaeology instead separates Korean states and communities, Krounovka settlements in Primorye, and Poltse traditions farther north. The digital start is a classification change, not the founding year of one people or government.

periods.title: 190 to 180 BCE: Wiman Joseon occupies only one corner
periods.summary: Wiman established control in northwestern Korea around 194 BCE, according to later written accounts. That polity matters inside part of the polygon but cannot name the entire peninsula, Primorye, or Amur basin. A documented ruler in one region does not validate the atlas umbrella.

periods.title: 180 to 170 BCE: Krounovka communities work inland valleys
periods.summary: Southern Primorye held numerous Krounovka settlements whose mixed economies emphasized farming alongside animals, hunting, and fishing. Site distributions and environmental evidence show local adaptation, not one map-wide subsistence recipe. Archaeological culture names organize patterns; they do not reveal every resident's language or ancestry.

periods.title: 170 to 160 BCE: Poltse and Krounovka remain distinguishable
periods.summary: Research at Bulochka treats Poltse and Krounovka traditions as synchronous but independently developed before later interaction. Dwellings, ceramics, tools, weapons, household objects, and ornaments record contact and change. They do not supply an ancient certificate identifying every maker as Tungus.

periods.title: 160 to 150 BCE: regional chronologies remain analytical tools
periods.summary: A national archaeological reference divides Amur Poltse material into stages extending before and after this card, while Primorye sequences use their own regional terms and dates. Period boundaries are scholarly tools, not universal event years. One atlas century cannot be pasted onto every settlement.

periods.title: 150 to 130 BCE: food systems mix crops and wild resources
periods.summary: Direct millet dates confirm long farming histories in southern Primorye, while regional reviews also document pigs, cattle, horses, hunting, and fishing at Krounovka sites. The balance changed by place and season. A grain find proves cultivation locally, not identical meals across seventeen polygon components.

periods.title: 130 to 110 BCE: islands and coasts connect wider exchange
periods.summary: Neukdo began during the second century BCE and later became an important maritime trade port. Dwellings, tombs, shell deposits, pottery, iron, and imported goods record coastal networks. Exchange linked communities without dissolving their identities or turning every harbor visitor into a Tungusic speaker.

periods.title: 110 to 100 BCE: conquest and a map repaint are different events
periods.summary: Han forces defeated Wiman Joseon in 108 BCE after war and internal division, transforming one political region. At 100 BCE the atlas removes Tungus everywhere, including places untouched by that conquest. One local political rupture cannot explain a synchronized disappearance across the whole polygon.

sections.title: Read the exact atlas feature before trusting its name

items.text: The index contains one exact tungus record, a circa culture from 200 to 100 BCE. It has one border feature, an imported modern summary, and no card or override. The separately deployed tungus-700 card belongs to 700 to 1000 CE and cannot be reused.

The decoded feature is a MultiPolygon with 17 components, 17 rings, and 666 positions. Its bounding box runs from about 123.75 to 141.26 degrees east and 33.19 to 52.69 degrees north. Sixteen small components are Korean islands, not footnotes that geometry may quietly discard.

Seoul, Pyongyang, Gyeongju, Jeju, Mudanjiang, Yanji, Birobidzhan, Khabarovsk, Komsomolsk, Vladivostok, Ussuriysk, and Nakhodka test inside. Shenyang, Changchun, Harbin, Blagoveshchensk, Nikolaevsk, southern Sakhalin, Chita, Beijing, and Dalian test outside. That odd selection is an atlas fact, not reliable ancient cultural geography.

The target shares one topology arc each with Paleo-Siberian hunter-gatherers, Xiongnu, Turcik tribes, and Han Dynasty features. Shared arcs explain how this digital map tiles space. They do not prove surveyed frontiers, treaties, ethnic edges, or guards stamping tiny ancient passports.

At 200 BCE the target replaces empty areas across Korea and Primorye, while neighboring points receive unrelated labels. At 100 BCE it vanishes and most former target probes become blank. Further repainting follows by 1 BCE and 100 CE. These are software seams, not coordinated migrations.

sections.title: Handle Tungus and Tungusic as later analytical terms

items.text: A Russian Academy study finds that Tungus became widespread as an ethnonym in Russian historical sources only during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Using it for 200 BCE therefore requires a warning label. It was not a demonstrated common self-name for everyone from Jeju to the Amur.

Modern Tungusic names a family of related languages, not a prehistoric passport. Researchers disagree over Proto-Tungusic chronology and homeland, with proposals ranging across centuries and regions. Language reconstruction can test relationships, but it cannot tell which language was spoken beside every uninscribed pot or hearth.

Reconstructed vocabulary may suggest ecology or practices, yet an academic review warns that a single reconstructed item cannot securely date a proto-language. Reconstructions are scholarly models assembled from later languages. They are not recordings, quotations, or labels recovered from a second-century BCE household.

The later tungus-700 card focuses on a much smaller Transbaikal-to-Amur sequence with Mohe and early Jurchen contexts. This exact card includes the entire Korean peninsula eight centuries earlier. Matching display names do not create matching people, shapes, sources, or chronology.

Nearby atlas umbrellas are equally unsafe shortcuts. Paleo-Siberian, Proto-Altaic, Xiongnu, Gojoseon, and Ainu cards each have distinct exact records and cautions. Their presence does not prove that this target was the missing piece of one tidy ancient ethnic jigsaw puzzle.

sections.title: Keep Korean, Primorye, and Amur histories distinct

items.text: Wiman Joseon emerged in northwestern Korea around 194 BCE and fell to Han forces in 108 BCE. Later court histories describe rulers, diplomacy, war, and internal division. Those events illuminate one region inside the shape, not a Tungus state governing southern Korea, Primorye, and Khabarovsk.

The atlas gives Seoul, Pyongyang, Gyeongju, Jeju, and many islands only the Tungus owner in 200 BCE. Its earlier Gojoseon card had already ended by 323 BCE, leaving a documentary and archaeological gap hidden by a single new color. The gap cannot be solved by renaming Korea.

Poltse I lies beside an Amur channel in the Jewish Autonomous Region. New radiocarbon work shows that most dated activity is later than this card's opening and that the particular settlement may begin after the exact interval. Evidence must follow the sample dates, not the atlas label.

Bulochka in southern Primorye preserves local interaction between Poltse and Krounovka material traditions. Researchers compare dwellings, pottery, labor tools, weapons, household utensils, and ornaments to trace change. Archaeological categories can overlap and mix gradually without becoming a single named nation.

Neukdo's shell mounds, tombs, and dwelling sites begin in the second century BCE and continue for centuries. The national heritage record anchors a real island community inside the polygon. It does not turn every other component into Neukdo or make maritime traders one ethnicity.

sections.title: Build houses, heat floors, and organize settlements locally

items.text: Excavated houses at Neukdo and Bangiri include early floor-heating installations built from stone tiles. Researchers distinguish L-shaped, U-shaped, and other forms across 49 dwellings. Their dates overlap this card, but one heating technology cannot identify a household's language, ancestry, or political loyalty.

Comparable heated floors occur at Krounovka sites in Primorye, where some examples may be older than those in southern Korea. The study proposes coastal transmission, a hypothesis rather than a household diary. Warm floors are an achievement; they are not an ethnic barcode.

At Poltse I, ten dwellings were arranged around central hearths with passages left toward exits. Vessels stood mainly along interior perimeters. That layout reveals movement, storage, fire management, and repeated domestic work, while leaving household membership and exact room rules unknown.

Regional synthesis records about 80 known Krounovka settlements in Primorye, concentrated in favorable inland areas before later coastal movement. Settlement density shows substantial communities and repeated landscape knowledge. It does not prove one central authority ordered every house or assigned every field.

Krounovka 1 contains many occupational phases, so excavators must separate deposits before comparing buildings and objects. A mixed layer can make centuries look like roommates. The cautious approach assigns claims to dated contexts and refuses to furnish one imaginary 150 BCE model home.

sections.title: Grow millet, keep animals, fish, hunt, and gather

items.text: Directly dated millet shows that farming had a long history in southern Primorye before this interval. The study also stresses changing combinations of cultivated and wild resources. Millet belongs in some local meals, but the evidence does not make one cereal menu compulsory across Korea and the Amur.

Krounovka economies included millet and other crops, pigs, cattle, horses, hunting, and fishing. The balance varied with local soils, coasts, rivers, and seasons. A household could farm and still fish or hunt, so modern labels like farmer and forager should not become rigid boxes.

The national archaeology reference describes Poltse communities as settled farmers who also kept animals, fished, and hunted. These practices are regional interpretations, not proof of Tungusic speech. A pig bone can identify an animal more confidently than it can identify the language spoken at supper.

Scientific analysis of Poltse pottery compares mineral composition, heating behavior, and crystal structure across Amur and Primorye samples. Those methods test production relationships more securely than appearance alone. A vessel's clay history still cannot identify its cook, owner, trader, or household language.

Neukdo preserves shell deposits together with dwellings and tombs, making marine foods and refuse archaeologically visible. Shell mounds record repeated activity, yet not every shell represents one meal or one household. Season, processing, trade, and later disturbance still need investigation.

sections.title: Make pottery, iron, tools, ornaments, and exchange networks

items.text: At Bulochka, changing combinations of ceramics, tools, weapons, household objects, and ornaments reveal interaction between Poltse and Krounovka traditions. Similar objects can move, be copied, or be remade. Style is evidence of connection, but it does not carry a tiny label naming the maker's ethnicity.

Use-wear analysis of Yankovsky stone tools asks what edges actually did rather than guessing from shape. That method matters even where iron appeared: older materials remained useful, and task-specific wear may reveal cutting, scraping, or processing. Tool function needs microscopic evidence, not adventurous storytelling.

Poltse pottery studies use petrological microscopy, thermal analysis, and X-ray diffraction to compare raw materials and firing. Those methods reveal skilled material choices without turning one recipe into a map-wide ethnic signature. Selecting clay, shaping, drying, firing, carrying, and repair formed a substantial technical chain.

Neukdo research tests three craft possibilities: making equipment for maritime work, adapting imported technologies for local use, and producing goods for exchange. Iron and pottery workshops could serve overlapping needs. A harbor was a workplace and neighborhood, not simply an ancient shopping mall with boats.

Bronze provenance research across Primorye finds diverse objects and long-distance connections with Manchuria and Korea. Chemical composition and artifact context can trace networks more securely than resemblance alone. Imported metal, copied form, and traveling person are different possibilities and should not be collapsed.

sections.title: See families, social life, children, and learning carefully

items.text: Poltse settlements could contain closely spaced semi-subterranean houses, indicating neighbors repeatedly sharing paths, work areas, smoke, noise, and maintenance. That setting supports cooperation, but residents cannot automatically be arranged into modern nuclear families. Kinship, marriage rules, and household membership remain questions, not floor-plan labels.

Heated floors demanded planning, fuel, cleaning, repair, and knowledge of smoke and airflow. Children could learn such work by watching and participating, but no exact-period lesson transcript survives. The archaeology supports skilled transmission; it does not reveal one school system, timetable, or universal age rule.

Neukdo combined houses, graves, shell deposits, craft activity, and maritime exchange. That mix implies neighbors meeting, working, eating, mourning, and hosting visitors. It cannot tell us every friendship or family joke, though a busy port surely produced more conversation than its surviving pots can repeat.

A southern Korean log-coffin burial contained a carefully built stone-packed pit, pottery, jade beads, and bronze objects. Mourners invested labor and selected particular goods, demonstrating remembrance and social distinction. One burial cannot define every family's beliefs, wealth, gender roles, or grief.

Krounovka-23 belongs to a landscape with many occupation phases, and its publication remains a local archaeological report. Children certainly learned speech, routes, farming, fishing, tool care, and social expectations, but the precise teachers, games, stories, and corrections are not preserved there.

sections.title: Discuss health, medicine, birth, and care without inventing them

items.text: At Boisman-2, Early Iron Age human remains appeared in the fill of a dwelling above much older burials. The report separates those contexts rather than blending them. That stratigraphic care is essential before using bones to discuss bodies, family groups, disease, or ritual.

The log-coffin burial shows mortuary care and selected objects, not a medical chart. Skeletons and grave goods may sometimes reveal injury, diet, status, or treatment, but this object page does not document diagnosis or healing. Funeral practice should not be repackaged as clinical evidence.

Millet grains and other food remains illuminate diet and farming rather than prescriptions. No reviewed exact-period source securely names a medicinal plant, dose, healer, or diagnosis across this polygon. The absence is documentary and archaeological; it does not mean people lacked plant knowledge or care.

No excavated lesson plan or birth manual survives from Krounovka 1. Pregnancy, childbirth, nursing, and infant care certainly occurred, but the consulted site record does not identify midwives, birth rooms, or universal customs. Honest uncertainty protects families from confident fiction dressed as reconstruction.

Krounovka excavation records houses and objects but does not reveal who soothed fever, set a fracture, or stayed awake with a sick child. Care was humanly necessary, while its exact techniques remain undocumented. A site catalog cannot safely be turned into a clinic register.

sections.title: Follow water, cleaning, waste, and the toilet question

items.text: Poltse settlements occupied high terraces near rivers and lakes. Nearby water supported drinking, cooking, fishing, travel, and fields, yet location alone cannot show whether a household carried, stored, boiled, or filtered water. Each step needs features, residues, containers, or other direct evidence.

Floor-heating channels managed fire and warm air beneath parts of a dwelling. They were not sewers. Archaeologists distinguish their stone construction, shape, and clay before interpreting function. Calling every channel a drain would give ancient plumbers credit for a system the excavators did not find.

Shell deposits at Neukdo preserve food waste and repeated dumping or accumulation, but a shell mound is not automatically a toilet. Contents, formation sequence, microscopic remains, and spatial relationships matter. Archaeology can identify refuse without pretending every discarded oyster knew the sanitation plan.

Excavated dwellings, pottery, tools, weapons, household objects, and ornaments all created broken pieces, ash, scraps, and worn equipment. Bulochka documents the activities and artifacts, not a settlement-wide sanitation code. Cleanup and disposal probably varied by task, season, household, and available space.

Toilet verdict: no securely identified 200 to 100 BCE toilet can represent this entire polygon. People relieved themselves and managed the result, but the reviewed Krounovka report supplies no standard latrine plan. Missing pipes are an evidence gap, not proof that everyone ignored hygiene.

sections.title: Treat writing, power, achievement, and continuity responsibly

items.text: No securely localized Tungusic-language text survives from 200 to 100 BCE inside the exact polygon. Proto-Tungusic forms are reconstructions from later languages, not quotations. This card therefore supplies no umbrella sample and does not borrow later Jurchen, Manchu, Evenki, or modern standardized writing.

A Chinese-style bronze mirror with writing is dated broadly around the first century BCE in the National Museum of Korea. Its characters show object circulation and Han-period writing, not a local Tungusic sentence. Uncertain find context and broad dating make it unsuitable as this card's sample.

Sima Qian's account of Chaoxian records negotiations, battles, officials, and surrender through a Han court historian's categories. It is valuable exact-period writing about one western Korean conflict, but it is an outsider political narrative, not the spoken voice of every community inside the atlas shape.

At 100 BCE the exact id disappears. Korean probes, Chita, and Ulan-Ude become blank, while several northern and western controls retain other labels. By 1 BCE Goguryeo, Silla, and Xiongnu labels appear at some points. None forms a single successor matching all 17 components.

Achievements belong to particular communities: heated floors, millet farming, river settlement, pottery, ironworking, maritime craft, exchange, and political negotiation. The later tungus-700 and tungusic-tribes records require their own cards. Historical continuity follows people and practices, not a traveling atlas label.

ending.text: The exact tungus feature ends at 100 BCE because the atlas removes its oversized umbrella, not because everyone from Jeju to Komsomolsk disappeared. Han conquest transformed Wiman Joseon in 108 BCE, while coastal exchange, Krounovka and Poltse traditions, farming, fishing, craft, family life, and local political histories continued on different paths. The next snapshots leave many former target probes blank and later introduce several unrelated labels. No single conqueror, successor, migration, or language shift explains the software change. The safest ending is therefore continuity with fell set to null and no asserted successors. The later tungus-700 and tungusic-tribes records remain separate chronologies and geometries rather than inheritors of this card.
